title: How Not to Build Microcrypt
authors: Aditya Gulati, Dakshita Khurana, Kabir Tomer
abstract: A key challenge in quantum cryptography is to build quantum one-wayness and pseudorandomness without the use of (quantum computable) one-way functions. So far, this has turned out to be a difficult task, with only a few proposed candidates that are not directly built from one-way functions. Even within these few proposed candidates, we have lacked the techniques to analyze when proposed constructions may inadvertently yield one-way functions.   In this work, we introduce efficient NP-aided shadow tomography of quantum states. We prove that collections of {\em computable} pure states can be learned via efficient NP-aided shadow tomography, where we say that a state is computable if the amplitude and phase on any computational basis term can be classically efficiently computed given the description of an efficient preparation circuit for the state. We also give new algorithms for NP-aided learning of unitaries given polynomially many queries to the unitary.   By building on this, we show that many existing architectures for PRS and PRU, including some that were explicitly introduced for the purposes of avoiding one-way functions (e.g., Hamiltonian Phase States, Bostanci et. al., TQC 2025), actually do imply the existence of one-way functions or imply \(\NP\) hardness. We hope that these no-go results will inform future investigations into building PRS and PRUs from assumptions that are plausibly outside the complexity class NP.
summary: This paper analyzes the fundamental assumptions required for quantum cryptography, specifically targeting primitives like PRS and PRU. By introducing NP-aided shadow tomography, the authors demonstrate that many proposed constructions inadvertently imply the existence of classical one-way functions or require computational hardness equivalent to NP. This work constrains the assumptions available for building quantum-secure protocols.
main_problem: The authors investigate the feasibility of constructing quantum cryptographic primitives, such as Pseudorandom States (PRS) and Pseudorandom Unitaries (PRU), without relying on the assumption of classical one-way functions.
main_result: They prove that many existing constructions for PRS/PRU, even those designed to avoid one-way functions, are shown to either imply the existence of one-way functions or imply NP hardness.
method: The work introduces and utilizes NP-aided shadow tomography and develops new algorithms for learning quantum unitaries, employing contradiction arguments based on posterior sampling techniques.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on computable pure-state families of quantum states and unitary transformations, analyzed through their measurement distributions and learnability by quantum computers with access to an NP oracle.
key_observables: Amplitudes and phases of quantum states, measurement distributions (classical transcripts), and the fidelity between estimated and true key states.
important_parameters: Error bounds ($\epsilon, \delta$), computational complexity classes (NP, BQP), and the structure of the underlying cryptographic primitives (OWSG, PRS, PRU).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of computable and samplable pure-state One-Way State Generators (OWSGs) and the ability to perform posterior sampling estimates.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the tools (NP-aided tomography, learning algorithms) and then applying these tools to show that specific classes of cryptographic candidates fail because they imply classical one-way functions or NP hardness.
why_interesting: While the focus is on complexity theory, the techniques developed for state learning and distinguishing quantum states from random ones are fundamental tools in quantum information theory, relevant for understanding the limits of quantum computation.
